extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and readers of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory textbook material describing U.S. federal institutions: naturalization rules, suffrage variation, judicial supremacy, and the organization and procedures of national party conventions and campaigns. Focuses on legal requirements, customary practices, and historical examples relevant to nomination and election processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts authorized to effect naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalization can be effected only in a circuit or district court of the United States, or a district or supreme court of a territory, or a court of record of a state having law or equity jurisdiction in cases in which the amount in controversy is unlimited, and having a seal and a clerk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the law of 1906 there are about 3500 courts which have power to issue naturalization papers; the process is under the general supervision of the Bureau of Naturalization in the Department of Labor at Washington.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial eligibility for naturalization (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only white persons and persons of African descent may be naturalized; the Chinese are excluded expressly by law, and this exclusion has been extended to the Japanese on the ground that they are not white persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the statutory and judicial restrictions in force at the time of writing; presented as an explicit legal eligibility requirement rather than a neutral policy standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage naturalization process
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalization falls into three stages: (1) declaration of intention on oath before the clerk at least two years prior to admission (applicant must be at least eighteen and renounce foreign allegiance); (2) petition for citizenship filed in applicant's own handwriting not less than two years nor more than seven years after the declaration (and after five years' residence), stating political fitness and verified by affidavits of two citizens certifying residence and good moral character; (3) final hearing after ninety days from filing, with renewal of declarations and judicial examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition must state that the applicant is not opposed to organized government, is not a public enemy, intends to become a citizen, and renounces former allegiance; affidavits from two citizens are required; the final examination may be 'formal or thorough and searching' depending on the judge, who must satisfy himself that all legal provisions have been complied with and that the applicant is of good moral character and attached to the Constitution. A large discretionary power is conferred on the court, and abuses by judges opposed to applicants' political principles are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency and documentary prerequisites for naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must reside at least a year in the state or territory in which he makes application; if he landed after June 29, 1906 he must present a certificate from the Department of Labor showing date of arrival, and the declaration of intention must be filed with the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural prerequisites (state residency, proof of arrival, timing of declaration) are mandatory parts of the application process and affect admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original constitutional allocation of suffrage to states
rubrics_metrics.description: The original Constitution contained no positive provisions relating to the right to vote but left the question to the states, stipulating that voters for members of the House of Representatives should have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the state legislature, and permitting state legislatures to decide how presidential electors should be chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus there is no national suffrage distinct from the suffrage of the respective states; state rules govern qualifications for federal elections subject to later constitutional amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendment constraints on state suffrage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments sought to protect the newly emancipated by providing that when the right to vote for specified federal and state offices is denied or abridged to male inhabitants 21 and over (except for participation in rebellion or crime) the basis of representation shall be reduced proportionally; and that the right to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although these constitutional provisions constrained states, the text emphasizes that a uniform manhood suffrage was not achieved and that enforcement of the Fourteenth Amendment's representation penalty had not been seriously attempted; political reluctance to enforce is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-level variations and restrictions on suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffrage varies by state: in nine states women were admitted to the suffrage; other states impose tax, educational, property, or other qualifications; some states permit foreigners who have announced their intention of becoming citizens to vote for state and even national officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These diverse restrictions operated to exclude thousands of adult male citizens across the country, not just in the South; examples cited include Massachusetts (educational test) and Pennsylvania (tax qualification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial supremacy and its role in protecting property and liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The supremacy of the judiciary is the crowning feature of the federal system: the Supreme Court can declare acts of other departments null and void and stands as the great defender of private property against popular legislatures; the judiciary acts as arbiter between the forces of democracy and property-owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from scholars (Professor Burgess, President Hadley) are used to argue that property status cannot be changed except by judicial consensus, constitutional amendment, or revolution; an independent, non-political judiciary is presented as essential to protect individual liberty from majority or party abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: National committee's pre-convention responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The national convention assembles on a call issued by the national committee, which meets usually five or six months before nominations to select the convention place and date and to issue a call inviting party members to choose delegates and alternates so the convention may be representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the eve of the convention the national committee completes preparations; at this preliminary meeting the programme of proceedings is determined and a temporary roll of delegates is compiled from state returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of delegates to the national convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The national convention is composed of delegates from the states and territories: each commonwealth is allowed two delegates for each of its Senators and Representatives in Congress (delegates-at-large correspond to Senators; others are district delegates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This apportionment does not account for the strength of the party in states (example: Mississippi with few Republican voters sent 20 delegates while Michigan with many Republican voters had 22); the text notes calls for adjusting apportionment to reflect party vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of selecting delegates: party differences and use of primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods differ by party: the Democratic party regards the state as the unit of representation and (in future) will require choice of delegates at primaries; the Republican party stipulates that delegates-at-large be chosen at the state convention and other delegates at congressional district conventions; special provisions are made for territories and states with direct primaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In several states in 1912 voters in party primaries were allowed to express preferences among presidential aspirants and the directly elected delegates were instructed to record those preferences at conventions—an early form of primary preference signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of the national convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The national convention formulates the party platform, nominates candidates for the presidency and vice-presidency, appoints committees to notify nominees, and organizes a new national committee charged with carrying on the campaign for four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-making, nomination, and organization of the party's national machinery are the convention's principal functions; platform language often consists of broad generalities intended to unite sections rather than specific policy commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention organization, temporary officers, and committee roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention begins with temporary organization (reading of the call, selection of temporary officers, adoption of previous rules), then appoints key committees—credentials (decides contested seats), permanent organization (names permanent officers), rules and order of business, and resolutions/platform (drafts the platform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The credentials committee typically hears disputes over delegations and its majority report is usually accepted; the permanent organization report usually names chairman and officers with minimal debate; rules follow House practice with modifications; the platform committee often seeks unanimity to placate factions, but minority reports can occur when issues are contentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominating procedure, roll call voting, and the unit rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations are made by roll call of the states; debate and speeches accompany nominations; voting is by roll call with the chairman of each delegation announcing its vote. Republican practice theoretically allows individual delegates to vote as they please; Democratic practice permits state conventions to instruct delegates and authorizes a majority in a delegation to determine how the entire delegation's vote is cast (the 'unit rule').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unit rule concentrates bargaining power in state delegations capable of delivering a block of votes; sometimes both delegations from a state are admitted with each member having half a vote to avoid rupture. The Republican nomination requires a majority of votes cast; the Democratic nomination requires a two-thirds majority—if no one achieves the required threshold ballots are repeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and composition of the national committee
rubrics_metrics.description: The national committee is composed of one member from each state and territory chosen by the respective delegations to the national convention and holds office for four years (from one convention to the next); the convention itself does not ordinarily control the choice of these members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the secretary reads a report of chosen members that is accepted unless objected to; the 1912 Democratic convention ordered the election of future committeemen in state primaries, indicating occasional procedural reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal officers of the national committee and their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal officers are the chairman, secretary, and treasurer. The chairman (usually the choice of the presidential candidate) conducts the campaign and must work closely with the candidate; the treasurer (often a financier) is responsible for raising the large sums needed to wage the campaign; the secretary handles records and administrative tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chairman's selection is important to campaign generalship; the treasurer may be chosen for financial influence and need not be a committee member. The candidate's wishes, committee preferences, and practical circumstances influence appointments; no absolute rules govern these selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign leadership, fundraising, and influence of financial interests
rubrics_metrics.description: After adjournment of the convention the national committee (led by chairman and supported by the treasurer) prepares and directs the campaign—raising funds, deploying speakers and organizers, identifying key states, and allocating resources to win votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives historical examples (Mr. Wanamaker in 1888; bankers' actions in 1896) showing how treasurers and financial backers can shape campaigns and how business interests may be appealed to for campaign funds; money and fund-raising strategy have decisive effects on campaign outcomes and political appointments.
